Status

Current state: Under discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: here

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

The teams that operate a Kafka cluster have no direct way to see how the clients connected to it are configured. In many organizations, the teams developing and deploying client applications are separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). As a result, an operator investigating a problem has to get the configuration from each application team, which delays the diagnosis and troubleshooting.

The gap matters because client configuration is a common source of problems. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. The gap impact gets more noticeable as Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, so centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. 

This KIP takes the first step in closing this gap by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Each client instance pushes the requested keys once, as soon as it discovers a broker advertising the feature, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance or framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. Most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps with one snapshot per client instance, carrying the identifiers needed to group it.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework can push one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does it with this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is collected is a default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name. A change reaches only clients that run their exchange after it, so running clients pick it up at their next restart.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers a one-time view of each client instance's configuration. A change to a client's configuration means a new client instance, which reports again. It delivers the hooks end to end: clients push what the cluster requests, the plugin acts on each snapshot and can give feedback on it, and the client reacts to that feedback as the cluster instructs. The cluster controls both: what is observed (requested keys), and how a client application reacts when the plugin rejects its snapshot (validation with modes: by default the application logs the cluster's feedback and keeps running. An operator can instead have it fail before performing any operation). No validation rule ships with this KIP, the hooks do, together with the client behaviour that handles their outcome. Overriding client configurations, and asking running clients to report again, are out of scope for now.

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds two RPCs, so that clients can send the configurations the cluster requests (keys and values), and a broker plugin interface, ClientConfigsPlugin, that receives them and can give feedback:

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : the client sends it to ask the cluster which configuration keys it requests. The response tells the client whether it must wait to push and get the cluster's feedback before its first operation.
  • PushClientConfigs : the client sends the values of the requested keys, once per client snapshot. The response carries the cluster's feedback and how the client application must handle it (e.g., log violations and keep running, or fail)

The KIP also adds:

  • broker and client configurations
  • one new error code (and reuses POLICY_VIOLATION)
  • broker metrics
  • one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams
  • a broker configuration client.configs.validation.mode, public enum ValidationMode,
    • this represents a config validation mode by which the operator decides how client applications react to the plugin outcome (e.g., snapshots for which the plugin may throw PolicyViolationException, see "Client Behaviour, Validation". No validation rule ships with this KIP
  • a ClientType field in PushClientConfigs, to be able to tell which client (e.g., producer, consumer, admin, share consumer), or which framework (e.g., streams), a snapshot describes

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3, which both new RPCs use. 

This KIP builds on top of

  • KIP-1313 (accepted) for the client instance id: both new RPCs introduced in this KIP use request header version 3, and the broker takes the client instance id that KIP-1313 associates with the request. A request whose header carries no valid client instance id (e.g., client library that does not follow KIP-1313) is rejected with INVALID_REQUEST.
  • KIP-1368 for the framework name, version and id in the plugin context. Given that KIP-1368 is still under discussion at the moment, we consider the alternative that without KIP-1368 those accessors return empty, and the impact is simply that a plugin cannot group the snapshots of one Kafka Streams instance.  Everything else in this KIP works as designed (the improved grouping capability could land independently).

The accessors are listed under ClientConfigs, ClientConfigEntry and ClientConfigsContext below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys. The client decides whether to send the config based on 2 main categories:

  • Sensitive configs
    • never sent by a client, even if requested by the broker. This filter is hardcoded.
    • it includes:
      • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
      • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
      • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • Built-in non-sensitive configs
    • sent if requested by the broker and not explicitly denied by the client (not matched by the client deny list configs.push.denied.keys)
    • it includes every key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys

Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client, so custom configs (keys in the client's configuration that it does not define, e.g., settings read by a serializer, interceptor or the application itself) are never sent in this KIP. The same applies to keys a client defines but does not support for its type or group protocol (e.g., session.timeout.ms defined for the consumer but not supported under the consumer group protocol, so a consumer using that group.protocol ignores it).
    • if a client sends a key it does not define anyway, the entry is typed UNKNOWN and the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behaviour).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value
    • each entry carries a Source field telling whether the key was set in the client's configuration or keeps the client's default
    • knowing the Source lets a plugin tell what an application changed from what it inherited (without knowing the defaults of every client library and version). It also gives a later enforcement KIP a place to mark values the broker applied (e.g., value 2 used in the future to tell that the config is "broker-enforced").
  • sensitive keys are filtered before any value is rendered. On top of that, the deny list supports prefixes to easily reduce what is sent
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client still sends a push with no entries, so that a plugin can tell a client with nothing to send from one that never reported
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are built-in non-sensitive configs:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in configs.push.denied.keys
    • key names and the sensitive-config rules are the client library's own
      • the default requested set uses the Java client's names
      • a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its sensitive-config rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behaviour: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name (client.rack included in the default requested set). An application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to configs.push.denied.keys.

Default Configuration for Apache Kafka clients

The default value for the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys  is one list for all client types. It includes:

  • identity keys that let a plugin group snapshots by application, consumer group, transactional producer or Streams application (client.id, group.id, group.instance.id, transactional.id, application.id)
  • client specific configs (all merged in a single list, defining the set of configs the broker/operator wants to "observe" from its clients, consumers, share consumers, producers and admins)
  • the list contains no class names and no custom keys

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • includes a single hook onClientConfigs
  • invoked synchronously with each snapshot the broker accepted (see Broker Behaviour)
    • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, validate, forward it, store it, etc. 
    • the implementation should return "quickly", running lightweight, in-memory work synchronously (e.g., validations), and offload heavier work asynchronously (e.g, forwarding, storage)
  • it may reject the snapshot by throwing PolicyViolationException
    • the client receives the error in the response, and how the client application reacts is the cluster's decision via the broker config client.configs.validation.mode (see Configuration -> Broker)
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation ships with this KIP (neither for observing nor for validating)
    • the KIP delivers the hooks and the client behaviour that handles their outcome
  • each snapshot reaches only the broker the client sent it to (or, after a retry, also the broker it retried on). The plugin stores it according to its needs, e.g., in a shared place such as a topic or an external store for a cluster-wide view
  • the plugin is not told when a client instance closes or restarts. A restarted client pushes again under a new client instance id. Some pushed identifiers can help a plugin link a snapshot to the same client after a restart, and expire the previous one: transactional.id and group.instance.id (default requested set), the KIP-1368 framework id for Kafka Streams, or client.id where the application keeps it unique per instance. Without one of these, old snapshots can only be expired by age

End-to-end flow

The following sequence diagram shows the interaction between the different components:


The flow includes the following steps:

  1. The client establishes a connection to the broker and sends an ApiVersions request
  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response
  3. From its network thread, the client sends a GetClientConfigsSubscription request to the least-loaded node that supports both RPCs
  4. GetClientConfigsSubscription response carries the keys the cluster requests and the broker's validation mode (Mode)
  5. If anything is requested, the client collects those keys (see "Configurations sent"), builds a PushClientConfigs request (with no entries if none survives the filtering) and sends it
  6. The broker checks the push (e.g., size), drops the entries the cluster did not request and any typed UNKNOWN, and calls ClientConfigsPlugin.onClientConfigs(), which returns to accept the snapshot or throws PolicyViolationException to reject it
  7. The broker returns the PushClientConfigs response as soon as the call returned or threw: ErrorCode NONE, or POLICY_VIOLATION with the exception's message as ErrorMessage when the plugin rejected the snapshot, plus the Mode
  8. The client marks its exchange as complete for its lifetime. These steps run on the client's network thread (triggered from they client constructors), and never block the constructor. The client's first operation waits for the GetClientConfigsSubscription response and, in reject mode, for the PushClientConfigs response (see Client Behaviour, Validation)" 

ClientConfigs, ClientConfigEntry and ClientConfigsContext

When the broker receives a PushClientConfigs push, it builds a ClientConfigs snapshot from the requested entries and a ClientConfigsContext. The context carries the request context, the client id, the client instance id (KIP-1313), the client type that this KIP adds to the push request, the client software values (KIP-511) and framework values (KIP-1368) from ApiVersionsRequest, the connection's address, the broker's receive time and the validation mode in effect.

ClientConfigsPlugin


No specific implementation ships with this KIP.

Exceptions

The broker checks the snapshot size before invoking the plugin. If it exceeds client.configs.max.bytes, it returns CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE with the limit in the error message. Other plugin failures are not reported to the client. A PolicyViolationException thrown by onClientConfigs is answered as POLICY_VIOLATION, reusing the existing error code and exception (no new exception is added)

  • determines how client applications react when the plugin rejects its snapshot (a PolicyViolationException)
  • values are:
    • warn: the client should log the feedback and keep running
    • reject: the client should fail before its first operation (see Client Behaviour, Validation)
  • cluster-wide value, carried as Mode in both responses

The plugin class and the size limit are static. The requested set and the validation mode are dynamic cluster-wide broker configurations (so they can change without a broker roll)

About rolls and restarts

  • enabling the feature is one broker roll (to set the plugin class) and no client restart. Every running client reconnects during the roll, sees the RPCs advertised for the first time, and runs its exchange.
  • a later change to the requested set is one command and no roll, but it reaches running clients only at their next restart (each client runs its exchange once). Operators should adjust the list before enabling the plugin.
  • setting the list empty stops collection with the same command and no roll: clients that start afterwards receive nothing and send nothing
  • changing the validation mode doesn't require a roll, and reaches clients that run their exchange afterwards: moving to reject does not re-evaluate running clients (a rejection they logged in warn mode applies at their next restart), and moving back to warn does not recover a client that already failed (needs restart)

Client

Applies to KafkaProducer, KafkaConsumer, KafkaShareConsumer and Admin clients, as well as Kafka Streams.

Notes:

  • proposing admin client default to false given that it's typically one-off operations, so for this common case each run would push a snapshot under a fresh client instance id (as opposed to producers and consumers that typically live as long as the application runs and carry the configuration operators want to see)
    • still, a long-running admin client can enable it (e.g. Kafka Streams does so for its own admin client)
  • no client-side allow-list: the cluster defines the keys it wants to observe from it's clients, operators can add/remove from that list, and the applications can only remove keys from that set. This is the initial approach as part of this KIP, future work could extend and add more client side flexibility if needed (e.g., to allow clients to push custom configs, out of scope for now)

Client API

One method is added to Admin, Producer, Consumer and ShareConsumer so that a framework can push its own configs through whichever client it embeds.

registerLogicalClientConfigs(String logicalClientType, AbstractConfig configs);]]>

Notes:

  • logicalClientType  becomes the push's ClientType . Implementations should pass the framework's name as KIP-1368 defines it, so a plugin can match the snapshot with the connection's framework name.
    • the framework id (KIP-1368) lets a plugin group the snapshot with the framework's other clients (e.g., the admin client, consumers and producers of the same Kafka Streams instance)
  • method to register is added to all four interfaces so that a framework can push through whichever client it embeds (same pattern used for registering metrics proposed by KIP-1076)
  • Kafka Streams uses it on its admin client to push the stream-specific configs through it

Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0. It uses request header version 3 (the headerVersions property KIP-1313 adds to request schemas), and the broker takes the client instance id from KIP-1313.


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse



PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response (that requests anything), the client sends one PushClientConfigsRequest per snapshot, from its network thread:
    • one push with its own configuration (ClientType set to its client type)
    • if a framework registered its configuration on this client, a second push with the framework's configuration (ClientType set to the framework name)
    • e.g., an admin client used by Kafka Streams would send 1 GetClientConfigsSubscription and 2 PushClientConfigsRequest (one with its own admin configs, one with the streams configs), or if Kafka Streams registers after the admin client's own exchange completed, a second exchange runs with 1 GetClientConfigsSubscription and 1 PushClientConfigsRequest to push the streams configs.
  • the exchange runs once per client instance (plus one more for a framework snapshot registered after it completed, see Client API)
  • the client retries only when no response arrives (see Client Behaviour), and any response ends that push
  • ClientType tells a plugin the type of client that the snapshot describes, and if it's the client's own configuration, or a framework's configuration pushed through the client.
    • reserved values, meaning the sending client's own configuration: producer, consumer, share-consumer, admin
    • any other value marks a framework snapshot and is the framework's name as KIP-1368 defines it (e.g., org.apache.kafka.streams)
    • null also means the sending client's own configuration, without saying which kind (for client libraries that do not distinguish client types). A library that does should use the reserved values
    • the Java clients always set it:
      • KafkaProducer sends producer, KafkaConsumer sends consumer (with either group.protocol), KafkaShareConsumer sends share-consumer, and the admin client sends admin
      • the admin client where Kafka Streams registers its configuration also sends a second snapshot with ClientType org.apache.kafka.streams 
    • the producers and consumers embedded in Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect send their own type (producer, consumer)
    • if not null: non-empty, at most 249 characters (same character rules as ClientSoftwareName in ApiVersionsRequest), otherwise the request fails with INVALID_REQUEST
  • Value is rendered as the Java client renders configuration values (ConfigDef.convertToString): LIST entries joined with a comma and no spaces, CLASS as the fully qualified class name, BOOLEAN as true or false, numbers in decimal, null when the value is null.
    • other client libraries should render values the same way, so a plugin reads a key the same whatever library sent it


PushClientConfigsResponse

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit. On POLICY_VIOLATION it is the plugin's message). This response is sent as soon as onClientConfigs returned or threw.

Errors

  • Both RPCs can return:
    • UNSUPPORTED_VERSION if the feature is off on the broker (no plugin configured), or the requested version is not supported
    • INVALID_REQUEST: if a request header has no valid client instance id (KIP-1313), or a malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit).
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the snapshot size exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end that push (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behaviour
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, leave client.configs.plugin.class unset (the RPCs are not advertised), or set client.configs.requested.keys empty to stop collection without a roll (see Configuration -> Broker).

For the client, set enable.configs.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behaviour

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • when receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker checks that the request header carries a valid client instance id (KIP-1313, INVALID_REQUEST otherwise) and returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys. The plugin is not invoked.
  • when receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • checks the snapshot size against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE)
      • checks that it's well-formed (e.g., including the ClientType)
      • checks that the request header carries a valid client instance id (KIP-1313), otherwise INVALID_REQUEST
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name.
      • this makes the operator's setting hold for every client library (considering clients that may not filter) 
      • the plugin is invoked even if nothing remains, with an empty ClientConfigs
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • no storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again
    • with this, the broker cannot tell apart a client that is older than this KIP or has enable.configs.push=false (sends neither request), a client whose push was rejected as too large, and a client that gave up after no response. Every client that implements KIP-1313 sends its client instance id, so a system that records instance ids can still list the instances that never pushed.

Configuration payload size enforcement

Clients only send the requested keys that belong to them, so a snapshot is small. As a backup, the broker checks the snapshot size of every PushClientConfigs request against client.configs.max.bytes before invoking the plugin. If the snapshot is larger, the broker answers CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE, with the limit in the error message, and nothing reaches the plugin.

A client's share of the default requested set is a few hundred bytes. The limit only matters if an operator requests every key a client defines. The table shows that worst case for the Java clients, so a default of 10 KB leaves room:

Excluding sensitive configurations

  • sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered (hardcoded sensitive set)
  • the broker does not check sensitivity
  • the broker only drops entries that are not in the requested set and entries typed UNKNOWN (see above)
  • a plugin may drop more (for example class-name keys); the client is not told about it

Client Behaviour

Exchange

The exchange runs on the client's own network thread (producer sender thread, consumer and share consumer background thread, admin client thread; for the classic consumer its network polling logic). It never blocks a user API call.

  1. the exchange starts when enable.configs.push  is true on the client and a connection's ApiVersionsResponse advertises both RPCs
  2. the client sends GetClientConfigsSubscription to the least-loaded connected node that supports both RPCs
    1. If RequestedConfigs in the response is empty, the client logs one DEBUG line and the exchange is complete.
    2. otherwise the client builds the snapshot from the keys that pass the filtering (possibly none, see Configurations sent) and sends one PushClientConfigs per snapshot (its own, and a framework's if one is registered, see Client API).
      1. when it sends the push it logs one INFO line naming the keys it pushes and the requested keys it filtered out, with the reason (sensitive/denied/not defined), never the values. With this an application can audit from its own log what left the process
      2. each push ends at its first response, success or error
      3. the exchange is complete when every push has ended
    3. if a request gets no response (e.g., disconnect, request timeout):
      1. the client retries it after retry.backoff.ms, growing up to retry.backoff.max.ms
      2. then continues retrying with backoff until default.api.timeout.ms elapses (config available for consumer, share consumer and admin but not producer). Producer retries capped at 3 attempts
      3. each retry goes to the least-loaded node that advertises both RPCs, preferring a node other than the one that did not respond. It goes back to the same node only when no other node advertising both RPCs is available
      4. if no success after all retries the client logs the failure at WARN and the exchange is complete
  3. the exchange is independent of the KIP-714 telemetry RPCs (GetTelemetrySubscriptions, PushTelemetry): there is no ordering between them, they may run at the same time, and they may go to different brokers
  4. the client only sends to a node that advertises both RPCs. If none of the known brokers advertise the RPCs, the client sends nothing and re-evaluates at each new connection (based on the ApiVersionsResponse).
  5. the exchange runs once per client instance (plus one more for a framework snapshot registered after it completed, see Client API)
    1. reconnects do not run it again
    2. later changes to the requested set are seen only by clients that run their exchange after it
  6. when a client is closed there is no specific action related to configs (it just drops pending config requests if there is any)

Kafka Streams

A Kafka Streams application reports its own configuration via its admin client, in addition to what its embedded clients report.

  • KafkaStreams calls registerLogicalClientConfigs on its admin client (one per instance), passing its framework name (KIP-1368) and its StreamsConfig
  • the admin client runs one exchange, or a second one for the Streams snapshot alone if its own exchange completed before the registration (see Client API)
    • when keys are requested, it pushes its own snapshot with ClientType=admin, and the Streams snapshot (StreamsConfig) with ClientType set to the framework name
  • all snapshots of one Streams instance (embedded producers, consumers, admin client, and the Streams snapshot) arrive on connections that carry the same framework id (KIP-1368), so a plugin can group them
  • enable.configs.push defined in a KafkaStreams application follows the usual Streams rules for client configs:
    • the value in StreamsConfig applies to every embedded client
    • a value prefixed for one client (for example admin.enable.configs.push) applies to that client only (overwrites the unprefixed one)
    • because the admin default is false, Kafka Streams sets enable.configs.push=true on its admin client unless the application sets it
    • if the application sets admin.enable.configs.push=false, the admin client sends neither request, so the Streams snapshot is not pushed

Kafka Connect

  • this KIP adds no Connect-level snapshot
  • worker and connector configuration is a separate surface (KIP-458 already governs which client configurations a connector may override) and is out of scope of this KIP
  • the workers' embedded clients answer the requested set like any client
    • they carry the framework name and version from KIP-1368 (and, for clients that serve a connector, its framework id), so a plugin can group or drop them

The feature will be covered by unit, integration and system tests, with a test-only logging plugin where needed. They verify that:

Rejected Alternatives

  1. A client-owned key set: per-client default lists, application override through config.push.allowed.keys, and a single PushConfig request with no way for the cluster to ask for anything. Rejected as this approach makes broker-side observability very limited, where the ultimate goal is to provide observability to broker/operator.
  2. A blocking handshake before the first user request. Rejected as it adds latency to the first request for no correctness gain (the broker learns nothing that it can act on sooner).
  3. A synchronous ClientConfigPolicy extending Reconfigurable, with a "process(...)" invoked on the request-handler thread. Rejected as "policy" implies validation the interface does not perform, also a synchronous call holds a request-handler thread for the plugin's latency. Rejected in favour of an asynchronous ClientConfigsPlugin approach, similar to KIP-1331.
  4. A broker-side sensitivity check: Rejected as the broker cannot judge key names across client libraries, and the client could not act on a violation since this KIP has no rejection semantics. Sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered.
  5. client_instance_id broker metrics and an instance-count gauge, were initially proposed in the KIP. Per-instance tags would bring unbounded cardinality, and the broker keeps no per-instance state to expire them with. Also an instance count has no clear value for an exchange that runs once per client instance. Both rejected.
  6. Omitting entries that hold their default value. Rejected because the push happens once per client lifetime and is a few kilobytes, so the saving is negligible. A plugin can drop default-valued entries itself.
  7. Never sending class-name keys (key.serializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes and similar). Considered initially, but they seems valuable, as they are a frequent root cause in client support cases. Also they only reveal package naming and the choice of serializers/interceptors/partitioners, but not credentials, endpoints or data. They are not in the default requested set, and an application can deny them.
  8. A ClientInstanceId field added to ApiVersionsRequest, considered in the first draft of this KIP. Not needed after KIP-1313.
  9. Others from the discussion thread on the initial KIP design:
    1. Sending the configurations as KIP-714 client metrics. Rejected because a configuration is a one-time snapshot of named values (many of them strings, lists or class names), while KIP-714 pushes numeric time series periodically on a subscription. Replaced by the two dedicated RPCs of this KIP.
    2. Sending every value as a plain string with no type. Favouring a type that lets a plugin interpret values without knowing each client library's configuration definitions. The type reuses the existing ConfigEntry.ConfigType, so there is no new enum to map.
    3. Sending custom configurations (keys the client does not define) when the cluster requests them. Left out of scope. A later KIP can add them with an explicit opt-in from the application.
    4. Giving a framework such as Kafka Streams its own client instance id and pushing its snapshot under it. Rejected because a framework has no connection of its own. Replaced by pushing the snapshot through one of its clients with ClientType set to the framework name. The KIP-1368 framework id groups it with the framework's other clients.
    5. Returning the requested keys in ApiVersionsResponse. Rejected because ApiVersions runs on every connection, while the list is needed once per client instance.
    6. Returning the requested keys in the push response. We did assess the push-response option as a single RPC serving both purposes (a push with no entries to ask, then a push with the values), but it seemed more confusing: two RPCs hidden in one relying on null/empty mode, with unused fields in each mode and one shared version range, error table and set of per-API metrics. KIP-714 splits exactly these two steps, so this KIP follows that shape at the cost of one more apiKey.

Motivation

The teams that operate a Kafka cluster have no direct way to see how the clients connected to it are configured. In many organizations, the teams developing and deploying client applications are separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). As a result, an operator investigating a problem has to get the configuration from each application team, which delays the diagnosis and troubleshooting.

The gap matters because client configuration is a common source of problems. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. The gap impact gets more noticeable as Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, so centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. 

This KIP takes the first step in closing this gap by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Each client instance pushes the requested keys once, as soon as it discovers a broker advertising the feature, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance or framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. Most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps with one snapshot per client instance, carrying the identifiers needed to group it.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework can push one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does it with this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is collected is a default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name. A change reaches only clients that run their exchange after it, so running clients pick it up at their next restart.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers a one-time view of each client instance's configuration. A change to a client's configuration means a new client instance, which reports again. Enforcing or overriding client configurations, and asking running clients to report again are out of scope for now.

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds two RPCs, so that clients can send the configurations the cluster requests (keys and values), and a broker plugin interface, ClientConfigsPlugin, that receives them:

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : the client sends it to ask the cluster which configuration keys it requests
  • PushClientConfigs : the client sends the values of those keys, once per client snapshot, without blocking its own operation

The KIP also adds:

  • broker and client configurations
  • one error code
  • broker metrics
  • one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams
  • a ClientType field in PushClientConfigs, to be able to tell which client (e.g., producer, consumer, admin, share consumer), or which framework (e.g., streams), a snapshot describes

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3, which both new RPCs use. 

This KIP builds on top of

  • KIP-1313 (accepted) for the client instance id: both new RPCs introduced in this KIP use request header version 3, and the broker takes the client instance id that KIP-1313 associates with the request. A request whose header carries no valid client instance id (e.g., client library that does not follow KIP-1313) is rejected with INVALID_REQUEST.
  • KIP-1368 for the framework name, version and id in the plugin context. Given that KIP-1368 is still under discussion at the moment, we consider the alternative that without KIP-1368 those accessors return empty, and the impact is simply that a plugin cannot group the snapshots of one Kafka Streams instance.  Everything else in this KIP works as designed (the improved grouping capability could land independently).

The accessors are listed under ClientConfigs, ClientConfigEntry and ClientConfigsContext below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys. The client decides whether to send the config based on 2 main categories:

  • Sensitive configs
    • never sent by a client, even if requested by the broker. This filter is hardcoded.
    • it includes:
      • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
      • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
      • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • Built-in non-sensitive configs
    • sent if requested by the broker and not explicitly denied by the client (not matched by the client deny list configs.push.denied.keys)
    • it includes every key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys

Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client, so custom configs (keys in the client's configuration that it does not define, e.g., settings read by a serializer, interceptor or the application itself) are never sent in this KIP. The same applies to keys a client defines but does not support for its type or group protocol (e.g., session.timeout.ms defined for the consumer but not supported under the consumer group protocol, so a consumer using that group.protocol ignores it).
    • if a client sends a key it does not define anyway, the entry is typed UNKNOWN and the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behaviour).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value
    • each entry carries a Source field telling whether the key was set in the client's configuration or keeps the client's default
    • knowing the Source lets a plugin tell what an application changed from what it inherited (without knowing the defaults of every client library and version). It also gives a later enforcement KIP a place to mark values the broker applied (e.g., value 2 used in the future to tell that the config is "broker-enforced").
  • sensitive keys are filtered before any value is rendered. On top of that, the deny list supports prefixes to easily reduce what is sent
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client still sends a push with no entries, so that a plugin can tell a client with nothing to send from one that never reported
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are built-in non-sensitive configs:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in configs.push.denied.keys
    • key names and the sensitive-config rules are the client library's own
      • the default requested set uses the Java client's names
      • a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its sensitive-config rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behaviour: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name (client.rack included in the default requested set). An application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to configs.push.denied.keys.

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • invoked asynchronously with each accepted configuration snapshot
  • it does not validate the configuration
  • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, forward it, store it, etc.
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation shipped with Kafka
  • each snapshot reaches only the broker the client sent it to (or, after a retry, also the broker it retried on). The plugin stores it according to its needs, e.g., in a shared place such as a topic or an external store for a cluster-wide view
  • the plugin is not told when a client instance closes or restarts. A restarted client pushes again under a new client instance id. Some pushed identifiers can help a plugin link a snapshot to the same client after a restart, and expire the previous one: transactional.id and group.instance.id (default requested set), the KIP-1368 framework id for Kafka Streams, or client.id where the application keeps it unique per instance. Without one of these, old snapshots can only be expired by age

End-to-end flow

The following sequence diagram shows the interaction between the different components:


The flow includes the following steps:

  1. The client establishes a connection to the broker and sends an ApiVersions request
  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response
  3. From its network thread, the client sends a GetClientConfigsSubscription request to the least-loaded node that supports both RPCs
  4. GetClientConfigsSubscription response carries the keys the cluster requests
  5. If anything is requested, the client collects those keys (see "Configurations sent"), builds a PushClientConfigs request (with no entries if none survives the filtering) and sends it
  6. The broker validates the push (e.g., size), drops the entries the cluster did not request and any typed UNKNOWN, and calls ClientConfigsPlugin.onClientConfigs(), which returns a future
  7. The broker returns a successful PushClientConfigs  response without waiting for the future
  8. The client marks its exchange as complete for its lifetime. None of these steps blocks a user API call

Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0. It uses request header version 3 (the headerVersions property KIP-1313 adds to request schemas), and the broker takes the client instance id from KIP-1313.


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse



PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response (that requests anything), the client sends one PushClientConfigsRequest per snapshot, from its network thread and without blocking any user API call:
    • one push with its own configuration (ClientType set to its client type)
    • if a framework registered its configuration on this client, a second push with the framework's configuration (ClientType set to the framework name)
    • e.g., an admin client used by Kafka Streams would send 1 GetClientConfigsSubscription and 2 PushClientConfigsRequest (one with its own admin configs, one with the streams configs), or if Kafka Streams registers after the admin client's own exchange completed, a second exchange runs with 1 GetClientConfigsSubscription and 1 PushClientConfigsRequest to push the streams configs.
  • the exchange runs once per client instance (plus one more for a framework snapshot registered after it completed, see Client API)
  • the client retries only when no response arrives (see Client Behaviour), and any response ends that push
  • ClientType tells a plugin the type of client that the snapshot describes, and if it's the client's own configuration, or a framework's configuration pushed through the client.
    • reserved values, meaning the sending client's own configuration: producer, consumer, share-consumer, admin
    • any other value marks a framework snapshot and is the framework's name as KIP-1368 defines it (e.g., org.apache.kafka.streams)
    • null also means the sending client's own configuration, without saying which kind (for client libraries that do not distinguish client types). A library that does should use the reserved values
    • the Java clients always set it:
      • KafkaProducer sends producer, KafkaConsumer sends consumer (with either group.protocol), KafkaShareConsumer sends share-consumer, and the admin client sends admin
      • the admin client where Kafka Streams registers its configuration also sends a second snapshot with ClientType org.apache.kafka.streams 
    • the producers and consumers embedded in Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect send their own type (producer, consumer)
    • if not null: non-empty, at most 249 characters (same character rules as ClientSoftwareName in ApiVersionsRequest), otherwise the request fails with INVALID_REQUEST
  • Value is rendered as the Java client renders configuration values (ConfigDef.convertToString): LIST entries joined with a comma and no spaces, CLASS as the fully qualified class name, BOOLEAN as true or false, numbers in decimal, null when the value is null.
    • other client libraries should render values the same way, so a plugin reads a key the same whatever library sent it

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit). This response does not wait for the plugin to run.

    • INVALID_REQUEST: if a request header has no valid client instance id (KIP-1313), or a malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit).
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the snapshot size exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end that push (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behaviour
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, leave client.configs.plugin.class unset (the RPCs are not advertised), or set client.configs.requested.keys empty to stop collection without a roll (see Configuration -> Broker).

For the client, set enable.configs.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behaviour

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • when receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker checks that the request header carries a valid client instance id (KIP-1313, INVALID_REQUEST otherwise) and returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys. The plugin is not invoked.
  • when receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • checks the snapshot size against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE)
      • checks that it's well-formed (e.g., including the ClientType)
      • checks that the request header carries a valid client instance id (KIP-1313), otherwise INVALID_REQUEST
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name.
      • this makes the operator's setting hold for every client library (considering clients that may not filter) 
      • the plugin is invoked even if nothing remains, with an empty ClientConfigs
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • no storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again
    • with this, the broker cannot tell apart a client that is older than this KIP or has enable.configs.push=false (sends neither request), a client whose push was rejected as too large, and a client that gave up after no response. Every client that implements KIP-1313 sends its client instance id, so a system that records instance ids can still list the instances that never pushed.

Configuration payload size enforcement

Clients only send the requested keys that belong to them, so a snapshot is small. As a backup, the broker checks the snapshot size of every PushClientConfigs request against client.configs.max.bytes before invoking the plugin. If the snapshot is larger, the broker answers CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE, with the limit in the error message, and nothing reaches the plugin.

Client Behaviour

Exchange

The exchange runs on the client's own network thread (producer sender thread, consumer and share consumer background thread, admin client thread; for the classic consumer its network polling logic). It never blocks a user API call.

  1. the exchange starts when enable.configs.push  is true on the client and a connection's ApiVersionsResponse advertises both RPCs
  2. the client sends GetClientConfigsSubscription to the least-loaded connected node that supports both RPCs
    1. If RequestedConfigs in the response is empty, the client logs one DEBUG line and the exchange is complete.
    2. otherwise the client builds the snapshot from the keys that pass the filtering (possibly none, see Configurations sent) and sends one PushClientConfigs per snapshot (its own, and a framework's if one is registered, see Client API).
      1. when it sends the push it logs one INFO line naming the keys it pushes and the requested keys it filtered out, with the reason (sensitive/denied/not defined), never the values. With this an application can audit from its own log what left the process
      2. each push ends at its first response, success or error
      3. the exchange is complete when every push has ended
    3. if a request gets no response (e.g., disconnect, request timeout):
      1. the client retries it after retry.backoff.ms, growing up to retry.backoff.max.ms
      2. then continues retrying with backoff until default.api.timeout.ms elapses (config available for consumer, share consumer and admin but not producer). Producer retries capped at 3 attempts
      3. each retry goes to the least-loaded node that advertises both RPCs, preferring a node other than the one that did not respond. It goes back to the same node only when no other node advertising both RPCs is available
      4. if no success after all retries the client logs the failure at WARN and the exchange is complete
  3. the exchange is independent of the KIP-714 telemetry RPCs (GetTelemetrySubscriptions, PushTelemetry): there is no ordering between them, they may run at the same time, and they may go to different brokers
  4. the client only sends to a node that advertises both RPCs. If none of the known brokers advertise the RPCs, the client sends nothing and re-evaluates at each new connection (based on the ApiVersionsResponse).
  5. the exchange runs once per client instance (plus one more for a framework snapshot registered after it completed, see Client API)
    1. reconnects do not run it again
    2. later changes to the requested set are seen only by clients that run their exchange after it
  6. when a client is closed there is no specific action related to configs (it just drops pending config requests if there is any)

Kafka Streams

A Kafka Streams application reports its own configuration via its admin client, in addition to what its embedded clients report.

  • KafkaStreams calls registerLogicalClientConfigs on its admin client (one per instance), passing its framework name (KIP-1368) and its StreamsConfig
  • the admin client runs one exchange, or a second one for the Streams snapshot alone if its own exchange completed before the registration (see Client API)
    • when keys are requested, it pushes its own snapshot with ClientType=admin, and the Streams snapshot (StreamsConfig) with ClientType set to the framework name
  • all snapshots of one Streams instance (embedded producers, consumers, admin client, and the Streams snapshot) arrive on connections that carry the same framework id (KIP-1368), so a plugin can group them
  • enable.configs.push defined in a KafkaStreams application follows the usual Streams rules for client configs:
    • the value in StreamsConfig applies to every embedded client
    • a value prefixed for one client (for example admin.enable.configs.push) applies to that client only (overwrites the unprefixed one)
    • because the admin default is false, Kafka Streams sets enable.configs.push=true on its admin client unless the application sets it
    • if the application sets admin.enable.configs.push=false, the admin client sends neither request, so the Streams snapshot is not pushed

Kafka Connect

  • this KIP adds no Connect-level snapshot
  • worker and connector configuration is a separate surface (KIP-458 already governs which client configurations a connector may override) and is out of scope of this KIP
  • the workers' embedded clients answer the requested set like any client
    • they carry the framework name and version from KIP-1368 (and, for clients that serve a connector, its framework id), so a plugin can group or drop them

Rejected Alternatives

  1. A client-owned key set: per-client default lists, application override through config.push.allowed.keys, and a single PushConfig request with no way for the cluster to ask for anything. Rejected as this approach makes broker-side observability very limited, where the ultimate goal is to provide observability to broker/operator.
  2. A blocking handshake before the first user request. Rejected as it adds latency to the first request for no correctness gain (the broker learns nothing that it can act on sooner).
  3. A synchronous ClientConfigPolicy extending Reconfigurable, with a "process(...)" invoked on the request-handler thread. Rejected as "policy" implies validation the interface does not perform, also a synchronous call holds a request-handler thread for the plugin's latency. Rejected in favour of an asynchronous ClientConfigsPlugin approach, similar to KIP-1331.
  4. A broker-side sensitivity check: Rejected as the broker cannot judge key names across client libraries, and the client could not act on a violation since this KIP has no rejection semantics. Sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered.
  5. client_instance_id broker metrics and an instance-count gauge, were initially proposed in the KIP. Per-instance tags would bring unbounded cardinality, and the broker keeps no per-instance state to expire them with. Also an instance count has no clear value for an exchange that runs once per client instance. Both rejected.
  6. Omitting entries that hold their default value. Rejected because the push happens once per client lifetime and is a few kilobytes, so the saving is negligible. A plugin can drop default-valued entries itself.
  7. Never sending class-name keys (key.serializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes and similar). Considered initially, but they seems valuable, as they are a frequent root cause in client support cases. Also they only reveal package naming and the choice of serializers/interceptors/partitioners, but not credentials, endpoints or data. They are not in the default requested set, and an application can deny them.
  8. A ClientInstanceId field added to ApiVersionsRequest, considered in the first draft of this KIP. Not needed after KIP-1313.
  9. Others from the discussion thread on the initial KIP design:
    1. Sending the configurations as KIP-714 client metrics. Rejected because a configuration is a one-time snapshot of named values (many of them strings, lists or class names), while KIP-714 pushes numeric time series periodically on a subscription. Replaced by the two dedicated RPCs of this KIP.
    2. Sending every value as a plain string with no type. Favouring a type that lets a plugin interpret values without knowing each client library's configuration definitions. The type reuses the existing ConfigEntry.ConfigType, so there is no new enum to map.
    3. Sending custom configurations (keys the client does not define) when the cluster requests them. Left out of scope. A later KIP can add them with an explicit opt-in from the application.
    4. Giving a framework such as Kafka Streams its own client instance id and pushing its snapshot under it. Rejected because a framework has no connection of its own. Replaced by pushing the snapshot through one of its clients with ClientType set to the framework name. The KIP-1368 framework id groups it with the framework's other clients.
    5. Returning the requested keys in ApiVersionsResponse. Rejected because ApiVersions runs on every connection, while the list is needed once per client instance.
    6. Returning the requested keys in the push response. We did assess the push-response option as a single RPC serving both purposes (a push with no entries to ask, then a push with the values), but it seemed more confusing: two RPCs hidden in one relying on null/empty mode, with unused fields in each mode and one shared version range, error table and set of per-API metrics. KIP-714 splits exactly these two steps, so this KIP follows that shape at the cost of one more apiKey.

Motivation

The teams that operate a Kafka cluster have no direct way to see how the clients connected to it are configured. In many organizations, the teams developing and deploying client applications are separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). As a result, an operator investigating a problem has to get the configuration from each application team, which delays the diagnosis and troubleshooting.

The gap matters because client configuration is a common source of problems. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. The gap impact gets more noticeable as Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, so centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. 

This KIP takes the first step in closing this gap by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Each client instance pushes the requested keys once, as soon as it discovers a broker advertising the feature, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance or framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. Most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps with one snapshot per client instance, carrying the identifiers needed to group it.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework can push one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does it with this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is collected is a default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name. A change reaches only clients that run their exchange after it, so running clients pick it up at their next restart.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers a one-time view of each client instance's configuration. A change to a client's configuration means a new client instance, which reports again. Enforcing or overriding client configurations, and asking running clients to report again are out of scope for now.

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds two RPCs, so that clients can send the configurations the cluster requests (keys and values), and a broker plugin interface, ClientConfigsPlugin, that receives them:

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : the client sends it to ask the cluster which configuration keys it requests
  • PushClientConfigs : the client sends the values of those keys, once per client snapshot, without blocking its own operation

The KIP also adds:

  • broker and client configurations
  • one error code
  • broker metrics
  • one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams
  • a ClientType field in PushClientConfigs, to be able to tell which client (e.g., producer, consumer, admin, share consumer), or which framework (e.g., streams), a snapshot describes

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3, which both new RPCs use. 

This KIP builds on top of

  • KIP-1313 (accepted) for the client instance id: both new RPCs introduced in this KIP use request header version 3, and the broker takes the client instance id that KIP-1313 associates with the request. A request whose header carries no valid client instance id (e.g., client library that does not follow KIP-1313) is rejected with INVALID_REQUEST.
  • KIP-1368 for the framework name, version and id in the plugin context. Given that KIP-1368 is still under discussion at the moment, we consider the alternative that without KIP-1368 those accessors return empty, and the impact is simply that a plugin cannot group the snapshots of one Kafka Streams instance.  Everything else in this KIP works as designed (the improved grouping capability could land independently).

The accessors are listed under ClientConfigs, ClientConfigEntry and ClientConfigsContext below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys. The client decides whether to send the config based on 2 main categories:

  • Sensitive configs
    • never sent by a client, even if requested by the broker. This filter is hardcoded.
    • it includes:
      • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
      • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
      • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • Built-in non-sensitive configs
    • sent if requested by the broker and not explicitly denied by the client (not matched by the client deny list configs.push.denied.keys)
    • it includes every key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys

Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client, so custom configs (keys in the client's configuration that it does not define, e.g., settings read by a serializer, interceptor or the application itself) are never sent in this KIP. The same applies to keys a client defines but does not support for its type or group protocol (e.g., session.timeout.ms defined for the consumer but not supported under the consumer group protocol, so a consumer using that group.protocol ignores it).
    • if a client sends a key it does not define anyway, the entry is typed UNKNOWN and the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behaviour).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value
    • each entry carries a Source field telling whether the key was set in the client's configuration or keeps the client's default
    • knowing the Source lets a plugin tell what an application changed from what it inherited (without knowing the defaults of every client library and version). It also gives a later enforcement KIP a place to mark values the broker applied (e.g., value 2 used in the future to tell that the config is "broker-enforced").
  • sensitive keys are filtered before any value is rendered. On top of that, the deny list supports prefixes to easily reduce what is sent
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client still sends a push with no entries, so that a plugin can tell a client with nothing to send from one that never reported
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are built-in non-sensitive configs:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in configs.push.denied.keys
    • key names and the sensitive-config rules are the client library's own
      • the default requested set uses the Java client's names
      • a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its sensitive-config rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behaviour: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name (client.rack included in the default requested set). An application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to configs.push.denied.keys.

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • invoked asynchronously with each accepted configuration snapshot
  • it does not validate the configuration
  • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, forward it, store it, etc.
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation shipped with Kafka
  • each snapshot reaches only the broker the client sent it to (or, after a retry, also the broker it retried on). The plugin stores it according to its needs, e.g., in a shared place such as a topic or an external store for a cluster-wide view
  • the plugin is not told when a client instance closes or restarts. A restarted client pushes again under a new client instance id. Some pushed identifiers can help a plugin link a snapshot to the same client after a restart, and expire the previous one: transactional.id and group.instance.id (default requested set), the KIP-1368 framework id for Kafka Streams, or client.id where the application keeps it unique per instance. Without one of these, old snapshots can only be expired by age

End-to-end flow

The following sequence diagram shows the interaction between the different components:


The flow includes the following steps:

  1. The client establishes a connection to the broker and sends an ApiVersions request
  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response
  3. From its network thread, the client sends a GetClientConfigsSubscription request to the least-loaded node that supports both RPCs
  4. GetClientConfigsSubscription response carries the keys the cluster requests
  5. If anything is requested, the client collects those keys (see "Configurations sent"), builds a PushClientConfigs request (with no entries if none survives the filtering) and sends it
  6. The broker validates the push (e.g., size), drops the entries the cluster did not request and any typed UNKNOWN, and calls ClientConfigsPlugin.onClientConfigs(), which returns a future
  7. The broker returns a successful PushClientConfigs  response without waiting for the future
  8. The client marks its exchange as complete for its lifetime. None of these steps blocks a user API call

Default: see "Default Configuration for Apache Kafka clients"

dynamic config (no roll)

The plugin class and the size limit are static. The requested set is a dynamic cluster-wide broker configuration (KIP-226), so it can change without a broker roll.

About rolls and restarts

  • enabling the feature is one broker roll (to set the plugin class) and no client restart. Every running client reconnects during the roll, sees the RPCs advertised for the first time, and runs its exchange.
  • a later change to the requested set is one command and no roll, but it reaches running clients only at their next restart (each client runs its exchange once). Operators should adjust the list before enabling the plugin.
  • setting the list empty stops collection with the same command and no roll: clients that start afterwards receive nothing and send nothing
